  A Git worktree allows you to attach multiple
  working directories to a single repository,
  enabling you to check out and work on different
  branches simultaneously.

  Traditionally, switching branches requires stashing
  uncommitted changes or committing incomplete work.
  Cloning the repository a second time avoids this
  but wastes significant disk space and requires
  duplicate network fetches. Git worktrees solve this
  problem elegantly by sharing the underlying object
  database, commit history, and configuration across
  multiple linked working trees.

  To create a new workspace, you run git worktree add
  <path> <branch>. Git immediately creates the target
  directory with that branch checked out, while your
  primary directory remains undisturbed. This
  workflow is ideal for quickly addressing urgent
  hotfixes, reviewing pull requests, running parallel
  test suites, or referencing another branch during
  active development without disrupting your local
  environment or triggering slow dependency
  reinstalls.

  Git also enforces strict safety rules: it prevents
  checking out the same branch in multiple worktrees
  simultaneously to avoid conflicting commits. Once
  you are finished with a temporary workspace, you
  can clean it up using git worktree remove <path>,
  and Git automatically prunes the corresponding
  metadata. Overall, worktrees provide a lightweight,
  highly efficient way to multitask across branches
  without painful, disruptive context-switching
  overhead.
